title: Viral Hepatitis Remains a Silent Threat as India Pushes for Elimination by 2030
excerpt: With over 21 crore people screened and 1,153 treatment centres nationwide, India's hepatitis programme has made strides — but chronic infections still kill silently, and experts warn the hardest gaps remain in awareness and early detection.
body:
• India has screened over 21 crore people and treated more than 6 lakh patients under its National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme, now in its eighth year.
  • Chronic hepatitis B and C infections cause no symptoms for years but can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer if left untreated.
  • Kerala recorded over 31,000 hepatitis A cases and 82 deaths in 2025 alone, highlighting ongoing sanitation and waterborne transmission challenges.
  • India's hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination coverage has crossed 92%, but only about 65% of pregnant women are currently screened.

India's Elimination Push Gains Ground

India marked World Hepatitis Day 2026 on July 28 under the global theme "Hepatitis: Let's Break It Down," with the Union Ministry of Health reaffirming its commitment to eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Eight years into the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP), the country now operates 1,153 treatment centres — exceeding the original target of one per district — and has screened more than 21 crore beneficiaries, according to data shared by Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava.

"India is among the few countries providing free-of-cost treatment for Hepatitis C and management of Hepatitis B, while continuing to improve access and affordability of services," Minister of State for Health Anupriya Patel said at the event. She noted that the cost of essential medicines has been driven below one dollar per course.

The Silent Progression From Inflammation to Cancer

What makes hepatitis B and C particularly dangerous is how quietly they operate. A person can carry the virus for years — sometimes decades — with no symptoms. During that time, the immune system's repeated attempts to fight the infection cause chronic liver inflammation, which gradually scars the organ. About 10% to 20% of people with chronic hepatitis C develop cirrhosis, and 1% to 5% progress to hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) over 20 to 30 years, according to research published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

"It is not uncommon for young adults in their 30s and 40s to be informed that their only treatment option is a liver transplant. Had it been detected earlier, it could have been managed with medication and monitoring."

— Dr Bhuvan Shetty, Consultant Hepatologist, Gleneagles BGS Hospital

Hepatitis B and C are spread through contact with blood and body fluids — unsterile injections, dental procedures, shared razors, or from mother to baby during birth. Hepatitis A, by contrast, spreads through contaminated food and water. All types cause liver inflammation, but B and C carry the highest risk of becoming chronic and leading to cancer.

Kerala's Recurring Outbreaks Expose Gaps

While India's national programme focuses on hepatitis B and C, hepatitis A outbreaks continue to devastate parts of the country. Kerala recorded over 31,000 confirmed hepatitis A cases and 82 deaths by the end of 2025 — the state's highest figures to date. Districts including Ernakulam, Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kollam have been most affected, with Ernakulam alone seeing a 390% surge in suspected cases.

"The increase in temperature and decrease in rainfall and decreasing surface water has impacted drinking water quality, heightening the risk of waterborne illnesses like hepatitis A," said Dr Lorance Peter, Director of Gastroenterology at Sakra World Hospital, Bengaluru. Health authorities responded by chlorinating water sources and inspecting food establishments in affected areas.

Prevention and Early Detection

The NVHCP has expanded screening and treatment to over 1.85 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs at the primary healthcare level. More than 7.64 crore pregnant women have been screened, and 2.24 lakh newborns born to hepatitis B-positive mothers have received Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 24 hours of birth.

Still, gaps remain. Only about 65% of pregnant women are currently screened for hepatitis B. Minister Patel urged states to push toward 100% coverage. The WHO considers hepatitis the second biggest cause of infection-related deaths globally after tuberculosis, claiming about 1.3 million lives annually.

What Comes Next

India's elimination timeline hinges on finding the "missing millions" — people carrying chronic hepatitis B or C who have never been tested. The NVHCP has integrated its case management system with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission to improve patient tracking and follow-up. Experts say the next phase must focus on expanding awareness in rural areas, strengthening occupational screening for healthcare workers, and maintaining India's vaccine coverage momentum as it works toward its 2030 goal.
nri_angle: Hepatitis B and C remain a health concern for the Indian diaspora, many of whom may carry chronic infections acquired before emigrating, and India's push for elimination affects families across the globe.
